source.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
source.authors: Maximilian Dreyer; Jim Berend; T. Labarta; Johanna Vielhaben; Thomas Wiegand; S. Lapuschkin; W. Samek

record.file_problem: The full paper and supplementary material are present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures semantic diversity in vision-network neuron examples and varies model/training settings, using SemanticLens interpretability scores rather than the original InceptionV1 neuron analysis.
record.gate_note: The study does not test InceptionV1 neuron 4e:55 or the cited cat-face/car-front/cat-leg examples. Relevant results are its own reports of polysemantic neurons and polysemanticity scores. Other results, including neuron-label accuracy, medical-model artifact sensitivity and ImageNet output AUCs, do not directly measure the claim versions and are not rows here.
record.test_reason: SemanticLens scores polysemanticity of vision-classifier neurons with a human-validated, embedding-based measure. It reports polysemantic units in pre-trained models and how the score shifts with architecture, dropout, sparsity loss, task complexity, augmentation and epochs. This is a different method aimed at the original question. It does not re-run the InceptionV1 analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right, but this is mainly a method paper. The authors introduce human-validated clarity, polysemanticity and redundancy scores. They find polysemanticity varies with architecture (higher in narrow ResNet18 and in ViTs), activation-sparsity loss generally lowers it, and dropout, epochs and augmentation have small, architecture-dependent effects. They also report that higher task complexity raised polysemanticity. They note the epoch results on the ImageNet subset conflict with their pre-trained-model comparison.
record.recipe_differences: SemanticLens collects highly activating examples, embeds them in a foundation-model semantic space and scores clarity/polysemanticity; it does not reproduce the original InceptionV1 neuron analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported polysemanticity scores vary with architecture, dropout, activation-sparsity regularization, task complexity and training epoch. The paper also says ResNet and VGG models respond differently to changes.
record.problems: The study's operational polysemanticity score is a proxy based on foundation-model embeddings and clustering. The authors note reliance on the foundation model and on concept examples being meaningful; the score experiments do not report corresponding task-performance costs. The narrow-model/capacity-pressure interpretation is not a direct causal test.
record.rows_left_out: No additional relevant numerical polysemanticity results were left out. Results on clarity, redundancy, augmentation and label faithfulness were excluded where they do not directly measure polysemanticity.

untested.parts: InceptionV1 and the specific cat-face/car-front mixture. The score is a continuous diversity measure, not a share of neurons responding to unrelated inputs.
Whole version: no count of features versus neurons and no capacity manipulation. The superposition link is only cited.
Task performance or accuracy cost of lowering polysemanticity; SoLU and modern convnets.
Effect of activation-range choice on polysemanticity classification.

missing.what: Pre-trained model comparison of polysemanticity scores across ResNets, VGGs and ViTs; values are only in the figure.
Data augmentation effect on polysemanticity (e.g., ResNet50 85.5 with none vs 90.3 with crop/flip), wrongly excluded in rows_left_out.
User study: the authors' cluster-based score correlates with human polysemanticity judgments better than clarity or clarity-increase scores, so classification depends on the scoring method.

record.verdict_notes: The polysemanticity score (1 minus clarity of two cluster means) is continuous, so values of 83-92% are not a share of polysemantic neurons. No uncertainty is given for the Table G rows except the dropout figure (8 runs). Fig. 5c says the sparsity loss improves interpretability overall. The reader's V3 support label was removed because superposition is only cited. A V7 label was not given because the user-study evidence is only in figures; it is recorded in missing.

versions.untested_parts: No InceptionV1 or neuron 4e:55 test; no direct test of the named cat-face, car-front and cat-leg mixture.
Language-model MLP neurons and token/context mixtures.
The study compares architectures and discusses narrow models as having a smaller neural basis, but does not directly count represented features or intervene on feature-to-neuron capacity pressure.
No test of polysemanticity caused by initialization, regularization or training noise when there is sufficient capacity for every feature.
The study tests vision architectures and selected training settings, not SoLU or modern convnets; it does not report whether regularization lowers polysemanticity without a large performance loss.
No causal test of whether apparently mixed neurons share a feature actually used by the network, or whether specific canonical mixtures resolve into one coherent job.

Although it varies sample counts and compares interpretability measures for other evaluations, it does not test how the measured prevalence of polysemantic neurons changes with activation-range selection or explanation scoring.

reader_labels.reason: The authors explicitly report components with multiple roles; this does not identify the named Inception neuron or show the roles are unrelated (r01).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.reason: The authors report higher polysemanticity in narrow models such as ResNet18 and interpret this as consistent with a limited neural basis and superimposed signals; capacity pressure itself was not causally isolated (r02).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Activation-sparsity regularization, tested models where the score falls clearly
reader_labels.reason: The polysemanticity score falls substantially for ResNet34 and VGG-13 (BN) with λ=80 (r07, r10).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Dropout leaves the reported score nearly unchanged for ResNet34, ResNet50 and VGG-13 but lowers it for VGG-13 (BN), indicating architecture-dependent effects (r03-r06).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Other regularization, task-complexity and training-duration results
reader_labels.reason: Sparsity and task-complexity effects vary in size and sometimes direction across models; the training-duration scores also vary by model and are mostly stable after early training (r08-r09, r11-r49). No performance cost is reported for these interpretability experiments.
